items.q: How did Java 8 change the way Java is written?
items.a:
Java 8's biggest turning point:
- [[g:lambda]] + [[g:Stream API]] (functional, collection-processing pipeline)
- [[g:Optional]] (reduces NPEs)
- default methods on interfaces
- [[g:java.time]] (immutable Date/Time API replacing the old bug-ridden Date/Calendar)

Java 8 is the longest-running LTS; many legacy systems still sit here.

:::deep
- Streams are [[b:lazy]] (only execute when there's a terminal op); `parallelStream()` uses the common ForkJoinPool — [[r:be careful]] with I/O tasks or when running inside a web container
- `Optional` is meant for *return types* to express 'may be absent' — [[r:should NOT]] be used as a field/param (anti-pattern)
- `java.time` is immutable and timezone-explicit (`Instant`/`ZonedDateTime`) — critical for multi-timezone OTA (local departure time vs UTC)
- default methods: evolve an interface without breaking implementers

[[r:Pitfall]]: overusing nested streams makes code harder to read/debug than a plain loop.

Trivia: lambdas do NOT compile to an anonymous class but to `invokedynamic` + LambdaMetafactory (class generated at runtime) → fewer generated classes.
:::

items.q: What does Java 11 bring that matters (compared to 8)?
items.a:
- `var` for local variables (type inference)
- standard [[g:HttpClient]] (HTTP/2, async) replacing the old HttpURLConnection
- run a single `.java` file without manual compilation
- removes the Java EE modules (JAXB, JAX-WS) from the JDK; G1 becomes default; adds ZGC/Epsilon (experimental)

This is the milestone many enterprises jump from 8 to in order to escape end-of-life.

:::deep
- `var` is just [[b:compile-time type inference]] (not dynamic typing) — still static, still type-safe
- new `HttpClient`: HTTP/2, async (`sendAsync` returns a CompletableFuture)
- [[r:this is usually where 8→11 migrations break]]: removed Java EE modules (JAXB, JAX-WS, CORBA) → must add the dependency yourself
- also introduces Epsilon GC (no-op, for benchmarking) + experimental ZGC

Deeper: the pain is mostly in removed modules/APIs and tightened reflection (illegal access), not syntax.

- Number worth remembering: 8 to 11 is the [[o:most painful]] step (Java EE modules removed, illegal-access tightened); 11 to 17 to 21 is mostly just bumping dependencies. Anyone still stuck on 8 should target 17 or 21 directly rather than stopping at 11 (02-java-8-25-java-vs-go.release-timeline.q7).
:::

items.q: How did Java 13–16 lay the groundwork for 17 (text blocks, switch, records)?
items.a:
The [[o:incubation]] phase — previews to gather feedback before finalizing in 17:
- [[g:text blocks]] (multi-line strings)
- [[g:switch expression]] (returns a value, no fall-through)
- previews of records, sealed classes, pattern matching for instanceof

:::deep
- [[g:switch expression]]: returns a value, arrow syntax, no fall-through, exhaustive → fewer forgotten-`break` bugs
- [[g:text block]] (triple double-quote): clean multi-line SQL/JSON/HTML
- records & sealed & pattern matching for instanceof went through preview in 14–16
- Helpful NullPointerException (14) points out exactly which variable was null

Deeper: the *preview feature* mechanism (`--enable-preview`) lets Java evolve quickly without locking in an API that isn't mature yet.

- Concretely: `switch` returns a value (`case A -> 1;`) so you can no longer forget `break`; text blocks let multi-line SQL skip string concatenation; `if (o instanceof Booking b)` skips manual casting.
- This is also why 17 (02-java-8-25-java-vs-go.release-timeline.q4) has no truly 'brand-new' feature: 13–16 already ran everything through preview, 17 just stamps it final.
:::

items.q: Java 17 (LTS) — what's the key feature set?
items.a:
- [[g:Records]]: immutable data classes, with constructor/equals/hashCode/toString generated for you
- [[g:Sealed classes]]: restrict the set of subclasses — tight domain modeling, enables exhaustive switch
- [[g:Pattern matching for instanceof]]: less manual casting
- strongly encapsulated JDK internals; numerous performance improvements

Java 17 was the recommended LTS throughout 2021–2023, and is still very popular.

:::deep
[[g:sealed + record + pattern matching switch]] = *algebraic data type*:
- enumerates every variant (compiler catches missing branches)
- immutable, exhaustive handling
- a great fit for state machines (booking: `Held | Paid | Issued | Cancelled`)

- Records generate equals/hashCode/toString for you, but remember to defensively copy mutable fields (List) in the compact constructor
- Java 17 tightens JDK internals encapsulation → 'illegal' reflection into sun.* is blocked, [[r:some older libs break]]
- the foundation for Spring Boot 3 (requires Java 17 minimum)
:::

items.q: Java 21 (LTS) — why is it a 'game-changer' for concurrency?
Java 25 (GA 9/2025) — what matters most for production and high-load systems?
items.a:
JDK 25 shipped 18 JEPs and is treated as an LTS release by most major vendors; the actual support duration, patch channel, and cost are [[o:vendor-specific]]. Important production-facing changes include:

- [[g:Scoped Values]] became final for immutable, bounded context propagation.
- [[g:Compact Object Headers]] became a product feature, reducing 64-bit object headers to 8 bytes when explicitly enabled; it is not the default layout.
- [[g:Generational Shenandoah]] became a product feature, but Shenandoah still defaults to its single-generation mode.
- Ahead-of-Time Command-Line Ergonomics and Method Profiling extend the AOT cache workflow to improve startup and warmup when the training run represents production.
- JFR gained cooperative sampling and method timing/tracing; CPU-time profiling is experimental.
- The KDF API, module imports, compact source files, and flexible constructor bodies graduated, while Structured Concurrency and several other features remained preview/incubator/experimental.

:::tip Production positioning
Java 25 improves memory density, observability, and warmup options, but none is a free universal win. Enable product features in a canary, compare application SLOs and resource use, and keep rollback-compatible flags. The Foreign Function & Memory API was already final in Java 22.
:::

:::deep
Compact headers reduce the header itself from 12 or 16 bytes to 8 on supported 64-bit configurations; application heap savings depend on object shape and alignment. Generational Shenandoah can improve workloads with many short-lived objects, but it must be selected explicitly and benchmarked against G1/ZGC under the same traffic.

AOT method profiles come from a training run. If production class paths, feature flags, or traffic differ, HotSpot still profiles and optimizes online; treat the cache as an optimization artifact tied to the build and workload, not as a replacement for JIT.

Structured Concurrency's JDK 25 API uses `StructuredTaskScope.open(...)` and still requires `--enable-preview`. Scoped Values are final. Mixing those lifecycle statuses is a common interview and migration mistake.
:::

items.q: Why do enterprises stick to LTS releases instead of the latest version every 6 months?
items.a:
“LTS” is a support commitment made by a JDK vendor, not a Java-language guarantee with one universal end date. Most vendors designate 8, 11, 17, 21, and 25 for long-term support, but free/commercial windows, platforms, update cadence, and backport policy differ.

Enterprises often standardize on a vendor-supported LTS because it simplifies framework certification, vulnerability patching, compliance evidence, and fleet-wide testing. That does [[r:not]] mean freezing the runtime: security and CPU/PSU patch releases still need a tested rollout path.

:::warn The migration risk is accumulated distance
Jumping from 8 directly to 21 or 25 combines language/runtime removals, strong encapsulation, library changes, TLS defaults, and build-tool upgrades into one programme. Regularly testing on the next JDK—even before adopting it—keeps the dependency graph and operational playbook ready. There is no universal “never fall more than two LTS releases behind” rule; derive the deadline from vendor support, security exposure, framework support, and migration lead time.
:::

:::deep
Choose an update policy explicitly:

- pin the vendor/distribution, architecture, support channel, and end date rather than writing only “Java 25 LTS”;
- apply quarterly security/critical updates through canary and rollback automation;
- run CI on the current production JDK and the next target JDK to expose warnings and removed APIs early;
- inventory preview/incubator flags separately because they offer no source-compatibility promise;
- rehearse rollback for runtime, container base image, agents, and native libraries together.

A non-LTS feature release can be reasonable when the team can upgrade every six months and needs a delivered feature. An LTS is a maintenance strategy, not proof that an application is secure or stable.
:::

items.q: Virtual Threads vs Goroutines — how do the models differ?
items.a:
Both are [[g:M:N schedulers]] that map many lightweight threads onto few OS threads, yielding automatically on blocking I/O.
GoroutineVirtual Thread
Introduced2009, mature schedulerJava 21 (Loom)
Stack~2KB growablecontinuation on the heap
Coordinationchannels (message passing)shared memory + StructuredTaskScope
Ecosystemwritten specifically for Goreuses JDBC/Hibernate/Kafka
Go's channels ≈ data passing; StructuredTaskScope ≈ task lifecycle management — they complement each other rather than being direct substitutes. :::deep - goroutines have their own scheduler refined over ~15 years (work-stealing, GOMAXPROCS, preemption since Go 1.14) - VTs mount/unmount on a carrier (ForkJoinPool); a continuation saves/restores the stack on block - coordination: Go favors [[b:channels]] (CSP, 'share memory by communicating'); Java favors shared memory + locks/concurrent collections + StructuredTaskScope [[g:Where Java wins]]: reusing the entire blocking ecosystem without rewriting it. [[r:Watch out for]]: pinning (synchronized/native) and heavy ThreadLocal use when there are millions of VTs (→ ScopedValue). :::

items.q: How should Java and Go performance be compared for a real backend workload?
items.a:
There is no defensible constant such as “Go uses 4–6× less memory” or “Java is 13% slower.” Runtime version, framework, GC, allocation rate, serialization, database latency, concurrency, warmup, container limit, and tuning can reverse a benchmark result.
MeasureControl before comparingReport
startup/readinesssame dependencies, image cache, probes, and cold/warm modedistribution, not one run
steady throughputsame response, dataset, connection limits, and target latencyRPS with p50/p95/p99 and errors
memory/densitysame container limit and load; include native/off-heap memoryRSS, heap/live set, OOM margin
costsame region, autoscaling policy, replicas, and SLOcost per successful business operation
Go often starts quickly and can have a small idle footprint; a warmed-up Java service can deliver strong throughput and latency, and virtual threads simplify high blocking-I/O concurrency. Those are hypotheses to measure, not language guarantees. :::warn Benchmark validity Drive the real dependency shape or realistic fakes, warm JIT-based services to the state production reaches, avoid coordinated omission in the load generator, and repeat until confidence intervals are useful. A GC that reduces pause spikes does not “eliminate” tail latency; queueing, CPU throttling, safepoints, network, and dependencies remain. ::: :::deep Make the decision from a bottleneck and total-cost model: - If compute cost is material, prototype the hottest representative service in both stacks and price the measured capacity plus operational headroom. - If database or partner latency dominates, language microbenchmarks may have no business impact; schema, caching, batching, and concurrency limits matter more. - Include team delivery speed, incident tooling, libraries, patching, and polyglot operational cost. A small runtime saving can be overwhelmed by a second build/observability/security ecosystem. Publish the harness, commit, configs, dataset, hardware, runtime flags, raw results, and date. Without that provenance, a number is an anecdote—not a reusable architectural fact. :::

items.q: When do you pick Java, when do you pick Go? What's the polyglot model?
items.a:
Choose Java whenChoose Go when
complex domain (many entities/rules)edge proxy, sidecar, CLI, infra tooling
need an ORM/mature ecosystem (Hibernate, Spring Data)simple high-throughput API
strong Java teamcost/container density matters
AI/LLM/vector integrationneed a single binary + fast startup
[[g:Polyglot]] is the dominant pattern in 2025–2026: Java for core business logic & stateful domains, Go for the edge/high-throughput layer; communicating over HTTP/gRPC (Google, Netflix, Cloudflare). The question isn't 'which language wins' but [[g:'which tool is right for each layer']]. :::tip Closing point Answering 'it depends on the layer' backed with cost/density numbers shows architectural and operational thinking, not language fandom. ::: :::deep - [[b:Java]]: complex domain, Java-first team (velocity >> the 13% gap), AI/vector integration - [[b:Go]]: simple HTTP+DB+cache at scale, single binary (sidecar/CLI/proxy), cost/service >$50k/year - [[b:Native Java]]: scale-to-zero/fast startup (serverless) [[r:The cost of polyglot]]: operating multiple stacks (build, observability, hiring) — don't go multi-language just because you like it. :::

items.q: GraalVM Native Image — which Java weakness does it address relative to Go?
items.a:
[[g:Native Image]] AOT-compiles to a native binary:
- millisecond-scale startup, small footprint, high density
- narrows the gap with Go for serverless/scale-to-zero

In exchange:
- peak throughput is usually [[r:lower than a warmed-up JIT]]
- more complex build process
- reflection/dynamic features need configuration

'Native Java' sits in the middle: better density than the JVM, lower peak than JIT.

:::deep
**Mechanism & cost:** AOT compilation under a *closed-world assumption* (every class must be known at build time) → reflection/dynamic proxies/resources must be declared (reachability metadata); Spring Boot 3 + GraalVM support this via AOT processing.

- [[g:Gains]]: millisecond-scale startup, small RSS, high density → great fit for serverless/scale-to-zero
- [[r:Losses]]: peak throughput lower than a warm JIT (offset somewhat by PGO at build time), longer & more complex builds, some libraries not yet compatible

Deeper: go Native when *autoscaling/startup is the SLO*; go JVM+ZGC when *p99.9 throughput* is the SLO.
:::

items.q: What's the future of Java: Project Loom, Valhalla, Panama?
items.a:
- [[g:Loom]]: virtual threads + structured concurrency — lightweight concurrency
- [[g:Valhalla]]: value/primitive classes — objects laid out 'flat' like primitives in memory, improving cache performance (data-intensive/AI)
- [[g:Panama (FFM API)]]: clean native calls replacing JNI; the foundation for C/AI integration

Direction: Java keeps its strong ecosystem while patching its historical weaknesses (concurrency, memory layout, native interop).

:::deep
- [[g:Loom]] (mostly final now): changes how I/O code is written
- [[g:Valhalla]]: 'flat' value/primitive classes (no header, no indirection) → better cache locality, less RAM (data-intensive/AI, large numeric collections); Java 25 lays the groundwork (Compact Headers)
- [[g:Panama (FFM)]]: clean, safe native calls (final since 22), the foundation for C/AI/SIMD (Vector API)

Deeper: these three projects are Java 'fixing itself' on three weaknesses relative to Go/Rust (concurrency model, memory layout, native interop) while still keeping backward compatibility.
:::

items.q: Records, sealed classes, and pattern matching combine to create what programming style?
items.a:
This trio brings the [[g:algebraic data types]] (functional) style to Java:
- [[g:sealed]]: enumerate every variant
- [[g:record]]: immutable data
- [[g:pattern matching switch]]: exhaustive handling (compiler catches missing branches)

A great fit for clearly modeling a domain/state machine with little boilerplate.

:::deep
**Practical application:** `sealed interface BookingState permits Held, Paid, Issued, Cancelled` + a record per state + exhaustive `switch` pattern matching:
- the compiler forces you to handle every state
- adding a new state and forgetting a branch → [[r:compile error]] (safe for a money/ticket state machine)

- unlike an enum: each state carries its own data (record fields)
- the [[g:'make illegal states unrepresentable']] style

Deeper: combine with deconstruction (`case Paid(var amount, var ts)`) for code that's both short and type-safe — close to Rust/Scala while staying pure Java.
:::
